reason: Tried to break it on translation drift, which is the real risk here, because three English renderings of section 92 circulate. Porter’s (1914) reads “A beginner ought never to have a second arrow…”; McKinney’s (Penguin 2013) reads “A beginner should not hold two arrows … You will be careless with the first, knowing you have a second. You must always be determined to hit the target with the single arrow you shoot”; and a web search summary wrongly labelled the McKinney wording as Keene. The shipped wording is neither of those. The Google Books volume feed, queried with three separate phrases from the line, returns Keene’s Essays in Idleness (Columbia University Press paperback, 1998) at p. 78 with the snippet “A beginner should not hold two arrows. It will make him rely on the second arrow and be careless with the first. Each time you shoot you should think not of hitting or missing the target but of making this one the decisive arrow.” I wonder if anyone with only two arrows…, all three sentences contiguous and verbatim (one line-end hyphen in tar-get is the scan, not the text). Shirane’s Traditional Japanese Literature (2007), p. 836, which reprints Keene, gives the same, as do two Prentice Hall anthologies. So the wording is Keene’s. The full printed page was seen only as snippets, not as a page image, and the 1967 first edition itself (Internet Archive bwb_W9-BRV-171) is lending-only and could not be searched; the 1998 paperback is a reissue of the same translation. It is a character’s line and the source names the speaker, the archery teacher, after the locator as the rule requires. shipped.js: not shipped, nothing near, Kenkō at 0 of 3, not banned. In scope (c. 1330, translation 1967), publishable, squarely on theme. Source line leads with the name, no dash, 95 characters. Tag Essay is the form (zuihitsu).
